claim: The rhesus macaque (Macaca mulatta) is likely the most widely used non-human primate species across biological disciplines.
source: Of all the non-human primate species studied by researchers, the rhesus macaque (Macaca mulatta) is likely the most widely used across biological disciplines.
evidence: This is a statement made in the abstract without specific supporting data or citations provided in that sentence.

claim: Rhesus macaques have the largest natural range of any non-human primate.
source: Rhesus macaques have thrived during the Anthropocene and now have the largest natural range of any non-human primate.
evidence: This claim is supported by Figure 2 which shows the geographic range, and is consistent with statements throughout the manuscript.

claim: Rhesus macaques are highly social.
source: They are highly social, exhibit marked genetic diversity, and display remarkable niche flexibility (which allows them to live in a range of habitats and survive on a variety of diets).
evidence: This is supported by the extensive discussion of social organization and behavior in the manuscript.

claim: Rhesus macaques exhibit marked genetic diversity.
source: They are highly social, exhibit marked genetic diversity, and display remarkable niche flexibility (which allows them to live in a range of habitats and survive on a variety of diets).
evidence: This is supported by discussion of SNP diversity and population genetic studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: Rhesus macaques display remarkable niche flexibility.
source: They are highly social, exhibit marked genetic diversity, and display remarkable niche flexibility (which allows them to live in a range of habitats and survive on a variety of diets).
evidence: This is supported by the ecology and diet section describing their range of habitats and diets.

claim: The first scientific paper on rhesus macaques described the anatomy of advanced pregnancy and was published in 1893.
source: The first paper described the "anatomy of advanced pregnancy" in rhesus macaques and was published in 1893 (Hart and Gulland, 1893)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hart and Gulland, 1893.

claim: A paper on behavioral cognitive experiments in rhesus macaques was published in 1902.
source: a paper on behavioral cognitive experiments followed in 1902 (Kinnaman, 1902)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kinnaman, 1902.

claim: The Carnegie Science Institute set up a breeding population of rhesus macaques in 1925 to study embryology and fertility.
source: However, the rhesus macaque really came to the forefront of non-human primate research in 1925 when the Carnegie Science Institute set up a breeding population to study embryology and fertility in a species similar to humans (Wilson, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wilson, 2012.

claim: Rhesus macaques were found to be relatively easy to keep and breed in captivity.
source: Rhesus macaques were found to be relatively easy to keep and breed in captivity and, at the time, they were also readily available via export from colonial India.
evidence: This is stated as historical knowledge without specific citation.

claim: In 1938, Clarence Ray Carpenter released 409 Indian-origin rhesus macaques onto Cayo Santiago.
source: In 1938, the American primatologist Clarence Ray Carpenter released 409 Indian-origin rhesus macaques onto Cayo Santiago, a small island off the coast of Puerto Rico, for behavioral research (Rawlins and Kessler, 1986).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rawlins and Kessler, 1986.

claim: The Cayo Santiago population has grown to over a thousand individuals.
source: This free ranging population has grown to over a thousand individuals, and has produced a wealth of research on rhesus macaque psychology and behavior that is likely unparalleled to our knowledge on any other primate species, with the exception of humans (Box 1).
evidence: This is stated as factual information about the population size.

claim: Rhesus macaques make up 65% of the non-human primate research subjects in the United States.
source: Today, rhesus macaques make up 65% of the non-human primate research subjects in the United States (Feister, 2018)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Feister, 2018.

claim: Rhesus macaques are likely the most studied non-human primate globally.
source: they are likely the most studied non-human primate globally
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the extensive research described.

claim: Rhesus macaques share a common ancestor with humans roughly 25 million years ago.
source: Rhesus macaques are Asian monkeys, sharing a common ancestor with humans roughly 25 million years ago (Ma; Perelman et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Perelman et al., 2011.

claim: The Macaca genus contains over 20 different species.
source: The Macaca genus is a large, geologically recent radiation containing over 20 different species (Fooden, 1976; Roos et al., 2019, Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fooden, 1976 and Roos et al., 2019, and Figure 1 shows the phylogeny.

claim: The Macaca genus diverged from other members of the primate tribe Papionini approximately 7 million years ago.
source: The Macaca genus diverged from other members of the primate tribe Papionini approximately 7 million years ago.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1 caption and the phylogenetic tree.

claim: The phylogenetic history of the macaque genus has been difficult to ascertain due to rapid diversification and significant introgression between macaque species.
source: The phylogenetic history of the macaque genus has been notoriously difficult to ascertain given the rapid diversification and significant introgression between macaque species (Liedigk et al., 2014; Fan et al., 2018; Roos et al., 2019; Osada et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations discussing phylogenetic challenges.

claim: Based on mitochondrial DNA sequences, Chinese rhesus macaques appear more similar to Taiwanese and Japanese macaques than to Indian rhesus macaques.
source: For example, based on mitochondrial DNA sequences, Chinese rhesus macaques appear more similar to Taiwanese macaques (Macaca cyclopis) and Japanese macaques (Macaca fuscata) than to Indian rhesus macaques, contradicting the taxonomic classification of the rhesus macaque species (Roos et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Roos et al., 2019.

claim: Based on nuclear genomic data, Indian and Chinese rhesus macaques are most closely related to one another, followed by Taiwanese and Japanese macaques.
source: However, based on the most complete nuclear genomic data currently available, a phylogeny of rhesus macaques and six of their most closely related sister species indicates that Indian and Chinese rhesus macaques are most closely related to one another, followed by Taiwanese macaques (Macaca cyclopis) and Japanese macaques (Macaca fuscata; Figure 1, Osada et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Osada et al., 2021 and shown in Figure 1.

claim: The discordance between nuclear and mitochondrial phylogenies is likely due to ancient admixture between Chinese rhesus macaques and Taiwanese and Japanese macaques.
source: The discordance between phylogenies created using nuclear genomes and mitochondrial genomes is most likely a consequence of the significant ancient admixture between Chinese rhesus macaques and Taiwanese macaques as well as Japanese macaques (Roos et al., 2019; Osada et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Roos et al., 2019 and Osada et al., 2021.

claim: Admixture between Chinese rhesus macaques and Taiwanese and Japanese macaques likely occurred during glacial episodes that created land bridges during the Pleistocene and early Holocene.
source: This admixture likely occurred during glacial episodes which created land bridges between China and Japan, and China and Taiwan, during the Pleistocene and early Holocene (Marmi et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Marmi et al., 2004.

claim: There is evidence for admixture between rhesus macaques and stump-tailed macaques.
source: In addition to the Taiwanese and Japanese macaques, there is evidence for admixture of the rhesus macaque genome and many other extant macaque species, including the stump-tailed macaque (Fan et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fan et al., 2018.

claim: There is evidence for admixture between rhesus macaques and Tibetan macaques.
source: the Tibetan macaque (Macaca thibetana; Fan et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fan et al., 2014.

claim: There is evidence for admixture between rhesus macaques and long-tailed macaques.
source: and the long-tailed macaque (Higashino et al., 2012; Yan et al., 2011; Bunlungsup et al., 2017; Ito et al., 2020; Satkoski Trask et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: High levels of admixture between rhesus macaques and other macaque species make them an excellent system for understanding ancient hybridization between hominin species.
source: The high levels of relatively recent admixture between rhesus macaques and other macaque species makes them an excellent system through which we might gain a better understanding of ancient hybridization between different hominin species (Boel et al., 2019; Buck et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Boel et al., 2019 and Buck et al., 2021.

claim: Rhesus macaques populate a range across more than 6000 km and 11 countries within mainland Asia.
source: Rhesus macaques, a relatively new species with many closely-related competitors, have come to successfully populate a vast range across more than 6000 km and 11 countries within mainland Asia (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 2 showing the geographic range.

claim: The current effective population size of Chinese rhesus macaques is estimated at 240,000.
source: The effective population size of rhesus macaques across their entire modern-day range is not known, but current effective population sizes of Chinese and Indian rhesus macaques are estimated at 240,000 and 17,000, respectively (Hernandez et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hernandez et al., 2007.

claim: The current effective population size of Indian rhesus macaques is estimated at 17,000.
source: The effective population size of rhesus macaques across their entire modern-day range is not known, but current effective population sizes of Chinese and Indian rhesus macaques are estimated at 240,000 and 17,000, respectively (Hernandez et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hernandez et al., 2007.

claim: Rhesus macaques have a substantially larger population than other closely related macaque species in Asia.
source: These countries represent only a portion of total rhesus macaques, but even those population sizes alone indicate that rhesus macaques have a substantially larger population than other closely related macaque species in Asia (Marmi et al., 2004; Bonhomme et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Marmi et al., 2004 and Bonhomme et al., 2009.

claim: Rhesus macaques have the second largest geographic range of any primate species except humans.
source: The large population of rhesus macaques is undoubtedly related to the extensive geographic area they occupy, which is the second largest geographic range of any primate species except humans.
evidence: This is stated as factual knowledge based on geographic range data.

claim: Rhesus macaque populations are not sufficiently distinct to warrant a multi-species designation.
source: While it is generally agreed that these populations are not sufficiently distinct to warrant a multi-species designation (Fooden, 2000 Pocock, 1932)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fooden, 2000 and Pocock, 1932.

claim: India suspended exportation of rhesus macaques in 1978.
source: India, originally the primary source of rhesus macaques for research, suspended exportation in 1978, and research facilities began importing rhesus from China.
evidence: This is stated as historical fact.

claim: Wright's Fst value between Indian-origin and Chinese-origin rhesus macaques is 0.14.
source: Wright's Fst value, a measure of the amount of genetic variance that can be explained by population structure, is 0.14 between Indian- and Chinese-origin rhesus macaques.
evidence: This is stated as a specific genetic measurement.

claim: Low levels of apparent admixture suggest that recurrent migration between Indian and Chinese rhesus macaque groups has been minimal over the past 1.6 Ma.
source: Relatedly, low levels of apparent admixture suggest that recurrent migration between the two groups has been minimal over the past 1.6 Ma (Hernandez et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hernandez et al., 2007.

claim: There are differences between Chinese-origin and Indian-origin rhesus macaques in disease pathogenesis, blood chemistry, the major histocompatibility complex, and aspects of behavior and temperament.
source: There are differences between Chinese-origin and Indian-origin rhesus in disease pathogenesis, blood chemistry, the major histocompatibility complex, and aspects of behavior and temperament (Champoux et al., 1994; Joag et al., 1994; Champoux et al., 1996; Binhua et al., 2002; Liu et al., 2008; Ma et al., 2009; Solomon et al., 2010; Jiang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Rhesus macaques have levels of single nucleotide polymorphisms that are exceptionally high among model organisms and approximately twice as high as those observed in most human populations.
source: Rhesus macaques have levels of single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) that are exceptionally high among model organisms and approximately twice as high as those observed in most human populations (Warren et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Warren et al., 2020.

claim: Functional genetic studies on rhesus macaques have identified specific genetic mechanisms underlying the timing of male natal dispersal.
source: Functional genetic studies on rhesus macaques have been used to identify specific genetic mechanisms underlying a wide variety of physiological and behavioral traits, including the timing of male natal dispersal (Trefilov et al., 2000)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Trefilov et al., 2000.

claim: Functional genetic studies on rhesus macaques have identified specific genetic mechanisms underlying the degree of female multimale mating.
source: the degree of female multimale mating (Trefilov et al., 2005)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Trefilov et al., 2005.

claim: Functional genetic studies on rhesus macaques have identified specific genetic mechanisms underlying the oxytocin response and maternal behavior in lactating mothers.
source: the oxytocin response and maternal behavior in lactating mothers (Wood et al., 2022)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wood et al., 2022.

claim: Functional genetic studies on rhesus macaques have identified specific genetic mechanisms underlying adaptations to cold climatic conditions at the northern edge of the species range.
source: and adaptations to cold climatic conditions at the northern edge of the species range (Liu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2018.

claim: Rhesus macaques persist over a range of environments including tropical and temperate climates, elevations from sea level to over 4000 meters, and forested, semi-desert, and swamp habitats.
source: Rhesus macaques persist over a remarkable range of environments: their niche includes both tropical and temperate climates, elevations from sea level to over 4000 meters, and forested, semi-desert, and swamp habitats (Neville, 1968; Lindburg, 1971; Goldstein and Richard, 1989; Richard et al., 1989; Liu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Rhesus macaques are found at the highest densities in non-forested habitat.
source: Although they are able to thrive under a variety of conditions, rhesus macaques are found at the highest densities in non-forested habitat (Fooden, 2000)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fooden, 2000.

claim: Rhesus macaques' most preferred habitat is an open environment with sparse tree cover.
source: suggesting that their most preferred habitat is an open environment with sparse tree cover (Richard et al., 1989).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Richard et al., 1989.

claim: Rhesus macaques developed their niche within 'disturbed environments' as a consequence of having evolved alongside frequent Pleistocene glacial episodes.
source: This is likely a consequence of having evolved alongside frequent Pleistocene glacial episodes, which resulted in rhesus macaques developing their niche within 'disturbed environments' - those with only partial or secondary forest growth, and, more recently, in urbanized environments (Saraswat et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Saraswat et al., 2015.

claim: Rhesus macaques attain adult lengths of 40–60 cm.
source: Rhesus macaques attain adult lengths of 40–60 cm, and weights of 4–10 kg (Fooden, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fooden, 2000.

claim: Rhesus macaques attain adult weights of 4–10 kg.
source: Rhesus macaques attain adult lengths of 40–60 cm, and weights of 4–10 kg (Fooden, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fooden, 2000.

claim: Among macaque species, rhesus macaques have a low to medium degree of sexual dimorphism in body size, with adult males being on average 51% larger than adult females.
source: Among macaque species they have a low to medium degree of sexual dimorphism in body size, with adult males being on average 51% larger than adult females (Turcotte et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Turcotte et al., 2021.

claim: Within the rhesus macaque species, body size increases with latitude across their natural range, with average male body size increasing 100% and average female body size increasing 75% from the southernmost to the northernmost point of their range.
source: In accordance with Bergmann's rule, which states that organisms at higher latitude should be larger in order to conserve heat, within the rhesus macaque species body size does increase with latitude across their natural range, with average male body size increasing 100% and average female body size increasing 75% from the southernmost point (15 °N) to the northernmost point (35 °N) of their range (Fooden, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fooden, 2000.

claim: Rhesus macaque populations in the Indochinese hybrid zone have smaller body sizes relative to their latitude due to recent introgression with long-tailed macaques.
source: One exception to Bergmann's rule occurs among rhesus macaque populations in the Indochinese hybrid zone, which has seen recent introgression with long-tailed macaques (see Evolutionary History), resulting in smaller body sizes relative to their latitude (Bunlungsup et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bunlungsup et al., 2017.

claim: Rhesus macaques are generalist omnivores with a highly varied and flexible diet.
source: Rhesus macaques are generalist omnivores, and have a highly varied and flexible diet (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 3 showing various food items and the discussion of diet.

claim: Rhesus macaques are primarily vegetarian and their diets typically reflect whatever food sources are predominant in their environment.
source: They are primarily vegetarian and their diets typically reflect whatever food sources are predominant in their environment (Lindburg, 1971; Tang et al., 2016; Zhou et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: In tropical and subtropical forests, rhesus macaques have been found to be primarily frugivorous.
source: In tropical and subtropical forests, rhesus macaques have been found to be primarily frugivorous, while in temperate and limestone forests they have been described as generally folivorous (Lindburg, 1977; Richard et al., 1989; Sengupta and Radhakrishna, 2016; Tang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: In temperate and limestone forests, rhesus macaques have been described as generally folivorous.
source: In tropical and subtropical forests, rhesus macaques have been found to be primarily frugivorous, while in temperate and limestone forests they have been described as generally folivorous (Lindburg, 1977; Richard et al., 1989; Sengupta and Radhakrishna, 2016; Tang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Rhesus macaques consume larval and adult insects, spiders, fish, crabs, birds' eggs, and honeycomb.
source: They will also consume larval and adult insects, as well as spiders, fish, crabs, birds' eggs, and honeycomb (Lindburg, 1971; Fooden, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lindburg, 1971 and Fooden, 2000.

claim: Geophagy is common in some rhesus macaque populations, potentially to prevent gastrointestinal disorders and as a mineral nutritional supplement.
source: Geophagy (the ingestion of soil or clay) is common in some populations, potentially to prevent gastrointestinal disorders and as a mineral nutritional supplement (Fooden, 2000; Mahaney et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fooden, 2000 and Mahaney et al., 1995.

claim: Rhesus macaques prefer foods that are easily obtained and consumed, but will shift their diet to less appealing or accessible food items when necessary.
source: Generally, rhesus macaques prefer foods that are easily obtained and consumed, but will shift their diet to less appealing or accessible food items (i.e. 'fallback foods') readily when necessary (Sengupta and Radhakrishna, 2015; Tang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sengupta and Radhakrishna, 2015 and Tang et al., 2016.

claim: Rhesus macaques thrive on agricultural and urban land.
source: While these same processes have caused the ranges of many other primate species to progressively shrink, rhesus macaques thrive on agricultural and urban land (Richard et al., 1989).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Richard et al., 1989.

claim: In agricultural areas, rhesus macaques have shifted their diet to cultivated crops.
source: In agricultural areas, rhesus macaques have shifted their diet to cultivated crops (Anand et al., 2018; Pirta et al., 1997; Rao et al., 2002)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: In urban areas, a considerable portion of rhesus macaque diet is either stolen from humans or intentionally provisioned by people for religious or cultural reasons.
source: and in more urban areas a considerable portion of rhesus macaque diet is either stolen from humans or is intentionally provisioned by people who offer food for religious or cultural reasons (Sengupta and Radhakrishna, 2020; Sarker et al., 2008; Teas et al., 1980).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Rhesus macaques likely have developed a preference for anthropogenic food because these are calorie-rich, easily digestible, and abundantly and predictably available.
source: They likely have developed a preference for anthropogenic food as these are calorie-rich, easily digestible, and abundantly and predictably available (Sengupta and Radhakrishna, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sengupta and Radhakrishna, 2018.

claim: Rhesus macaques are categorized as 'Least Concern' on the IUCN Red List.
source: Being categorized as 'Least Concern' on the IUCN Red List effectively excludes rhesus macaques from many conservation plans.
evidence: This is stated as factual information about conservation status.

claim: Rhesus macaques live in multi-male multi-female groups with a polygynandrous mating system.
source: Rhesus macaques live in multi-male multi-female groups with a polygynandrous mating system.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about their social organization.

claim: Rhesus macaque groups have a female-biased adult sex ratio with on average one mature male per three mature females per group.
source: Groups have a female-biased adult sex ratio; on average there is one mature male per three mature females per group (Fooden, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fooden, 2000.

claim: Male rhesus macaques disperse from their natal group to join a neighboring group around the time they reach sexual maturity.
source: Male rhesus macaques disperse from their natal group to join a neighboring group around the time they reach sexual maturity, but females typically remain in their natal group for their entire lives, such that social groups are stably composed of matrilines (i.e. families of females related through the maternal line; Neville, 1968; Lindburg, 1971; Sade, 1972; Teas et al., 1980; Maestripieri and Hoffman, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Female rhesus macaques typically remain in their natal group for their entire lives.
source: Male rhesus macaques disperse from their natal group to join a neighboring group around the time they reach sexual maturity, but females typically remain in their natal group for their entire lives, such that social groups are stably composed of matrilines (i.e. families of females related through the maternal line; Neville, 1968; Lindburg, 1971; Sade, 1972; Teas et al., 1980; Maestripieri and Hoffman, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Male rhesus macaque group membership is not fixed through adulthood, as males will periodically leave one group to join another.
source: Male group membership is not fixed through adulthood, as males will periodically leave one group to join another, and sometimes males will not be affiliated with any group at all (see Box 2 Q3; Lindburg, 1969; Boelkins and Wilson, 1972; Drickamer and Vessey, 1973).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: For non-provisioned and minimally-provisioned wild rhesus macaques, the average group size is 32 and the maximum recorded is 250.
source: Fooden, 2000 synthesized studies from nine countries across a range of habitat types which included 1188 rhesus macaque groups and found that for non-provisioned and minimally-provisioned wild rhesus macaques the average group size was 32, and the maximum recorded was 250.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fooden, 2000.

claim: Food provisioning of wild rhesus macaque populations results in a substantial increase in group size, with the average being 77 and the maximum recorded being 1045 individuals.
source: Food provisioning of wild populations results in a substantial increase in group size, with the average being 77 and the maximum recorded being 1045 individuals (Fooden, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fooden, 2000.

claim: Home ranges between adjacent rhesus macaque groups typically overlap.
source: Home ranges between adjacent groups typically overlap, and group fissions will occasionally happen and typically occur along matrilines, with female family members almost always staying together (Lindburg, 1971; Widdig et al., 2006; Sueur et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Group fissions in rhesus macaques typically occur along matrilines, with female family members almost always staying together.
source: Home ranges between adjacent groups typically overlap, and group fissions will occasionally happen and typically occur along matrilines, with female family members almost always staying together (Lindburg, 1971; Widdig et al., 2006; Sueur et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Rhesus macaques are notable for their high frequency and severity of aggression and absence of reconciliation between conspecifics when compared to other macaque species.
source: Rhesus macaques are notable for their high frequency and severity of aggression and absence of reconciliation between conspecifics when compared to other macaque species, which leads to a social organization that can be described as both highly "despotic and nepotistic" (Thierry, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Thierry, 2007.

claim: Steep linear dominance hierarchies are formed within a rhesus macaque social group, for both males and females separately.
source: Steep linear dominance hierarchies are formed within a social group, for both males and females separately (Datta, 1988; Missakian, 1972).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Datta, 1988 and Missakian, 1972.

claim: For female rhesus macaques, dominance rank is relatively stable and is determined first by matrilineal group, and second by age, with younger females outranking their older sisters.
source: For females, dominance rank is relatively stable and is determined first by matrilineal group, and second by age, with younger females outranking their older sisters (Berman, 1986; Missakian, 1972).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Berman, 1986 and Missakian, 1972.

claim: When male rhesus macaques immigrate to a new social group they generally enter at the bottom of the social hierarchy and rise through queuing, such that group tenure-length is the primary determinant of male rank.
source: When males immigrate to a new social group they generally enter at the bottom of the social hierarchy and rise through queuing, such that group tenure-length is the primary determinant of male rank (Manson, 1998; Maestripieri and Hoffman, 2012; Higham and Maestripieri, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Male rhesus macaques rising in dominance rank through coalitionary aggression is thought to be rare.
source: There have been occasional observations of male rhesus macaques rising in dominance rank through coalitionary aggression, but these are thought to be rare (Higham and Maestripieri, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Higham and Maestripieri, 2010.

claim: In female rhesus macaques, higher dominance rank has been associated with greater annual fertility, survival, earlier maturation of up to half a year, and shorter inter-birth interval.
source: In females, higher dominance rank has been associated with greater annual fertility, survival, earlier maturation of up to half a year, and shorter inter-birth interval (Drickamer, 1974; Bercovitch and Berard, 1993; Blomquist, 2009; Blomquist et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: In male rhesus macaques, dominance rank is positively correlated with mating and reproductive success, but this can be highly variable by population and year.
source: In males, dominance rank is positively correlated with mating and reproductive success, but this can be highly variable by population and year (Manson, 1992; Bercovitch and Nürnberg, 1997; Berard, 1999; Widdig et al., 2004; Dubuc et al., 2011; Dubuc et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Various measures of social stability, integration, and connectedness have been shown to affect a wide variety of physiological metrics in rhesus macaques, including the sympathetic nervous system, white blood cell count and fecal glucocorticoid concentrations.
source: Various measures of social stability, integration, and connectedness have been shown to affect a wide variety of physiological metrics in rhesus macaques, including the sympathetic nervous system, white blood cell count and fecal glucocorticoid concentrations (Capitanio and Cole, 2015; Pavez-Fox et al., 2021; Brent et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Measures of increased social affiliation are positively related to both reproductive output and survival probability in rhesus macaques.
source: As in a number of other primate species (e.g. Silk, 2007), measures of increased social affiliation are positively related to both reproductive output and survival probability (Brent et al., 2013; Ellis et al., 2019; Brent et al., 2017a).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Rhesus macaque early-life adversity is predictive of both sociality variables in adulthood, such as rates of aggression, as well as physiological metrics including hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis dysregulation.
source: Rhesus macaque early-life adversity is predictive of both sociality variables in adulthood, such as rates of aggression, as well as physiological metrics that may be associated with health and fitness including hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis dysregulation (Barr et al., 2003; Dettmer et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Barr et al., 2003 and Dettmer et al., 2017.

claim: Rhesus macaque early-life adversity is predictive of DNA methylation profile.
source: and DNA methylation profile (Massart et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Massart et al., 2016.

claim: Rhesus macaques are considered 'relaxed income breeders' in that they display primarily the characteristics of 'income breeders', but endogenous conditions such as body mass do play some role in determining reproductive success.
source: Rhesus macaques are considered 'relaxed income breeders' in that they display primarily the characteristics of 'income breeders', but they are not 'strict' in the sense that endogenous conditions such as body mass do play some role in determining reproductive success (Brockman, 2005; Tian et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Brockman, 2005 and Tian et al., 2013.

claim: Rhesus macaques time birth and lactation with the months of the year where food availability is highest.
source: As income breeders, rhesus macaques time birth and lactation with the months of the year where food availability is highest, as they require the highest energetic intake during this time.
evidence: This is inferred from the income breeder characterization.

claim: Rhesus macaque mating occurs approximately in the fall and winter, and the birth season occurs over the spring and summer.
source: Consequently, mating occurs approximately in the fall and winter, and the birth season occurs over the spring and summer (Fooden, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fooden, 2000.

claim: A group of rhesus macaques which were breeding seasonally at Cayo Santiago lost seasonality when brought to German Primate Center at Gottingen and housed in controlled temperature and photoperiods, but seasonality reappeared when the group was released into a large outdoor enclosure.
source: Interestingly, a group of rhesus macaques which were breeding seasonally at Cayo Santiago lost seasonality when brought to German Primate Center at Gottingen and housed in controlled temperature and photoperiods. However, in the subsequent years when the group was released into a large outdoor enclosure, seasonality reappeared (Kaumanns et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kaumanns et al., 2013.

claim: The combination of large group sizes and reproductive seasonality leads to females within a rhesus macaque population displaying synchrony in their fertility cycles.
source: The combination of large group sizes and reproductive seasonality leads to females within a population displaying synchrony in their fertility cycles and is thought to be the driver of weak direct male-male competition, such as through physical combat, and strong indirect male-male competition, such as through female mate choice (Gogarten and Koenig, 2013; Kutsukake and Nunn, 2009; Ostner et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: High female fertile phase synchrony in rhesus macaques lowers the ability for males to monopolize females, creating a relatively weak competitive environment which leads to relatively low male reproductive skew.
source: High female fertile phase synchrony lowers the ability for males to monopolize females, creating a relatively weak competitive environment which leads to relatively low male reproductive skew where reproductive success is not monopolized by only one or a small number of males, and selects for limited body and canine size dimorphism and large relative testis volume (Dubuc et al., 2014b; Harcourt et al., 1981; Dubuc et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Rhesus macaques exhibit strong evidence of direct female mate choice, with females playing an active role in soliciting mating from a preferred partner.
source: Rhesus macaques exhibit strong evidence of direct female mate choice, with females playing an active role in soliciting mating from a preferred partner (Maestripieri and Hoffman, 2012; Bercovitch, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Maestripieri and Hoffman, 2012 and Bercovitch, 1997.

claim: Female rhesus macaques prefer to mate with novel males, middle-aged males, and males with darker red faces.
source: Females prefer to mate with novel males (i.e. those that have recently immigrated to their social group), middle-aged males, and males with darker red faces (Maestripieri and Hoffman, 2012; Dubuc et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Maestripieri and Hoffman, 2012 and Dubuc et al., 2014a.

claim: Female rhesus macaques will typically enter multiple ovarian cycles during the mating season, each lasting 30 days.
source: Females will typically enter multiple ovarian cycles during the mating season, each lasting 30 days.
evidence: This is stated as factual information about reproductive physiology.

claim: Consortships lasting several hours to several days are formed between a fertile female rhesus macaque and a male partner.
source: Consortships lasting several hours to several days are formed between a fertile female and a male partner; the pair remains in close proximity during which time the pair engages in multi-mount copulations (Bercovitch, 1997; Higham et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bercovitch, 1997 and Higham et al., 2011.

claim: Female rhesus macaques are likely to have more than one male consort, averaging three to four mating partners within a single fertile period.
source: Females are likely to have more than one male consort, averaging three to four mating partners within a single fertile period (Manson, 1992; Lindburg, 1971; Bercovitch, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Male rhesus macaques with higher dominance rank engage in consorts of longer duration, while lower ranking males will either engage in shorter consorts or 'sneak' matings.
source: Males with higher dominance rank engage in consorts of longer duration, while lower ranking males will either engage in shorter consorts or 'sneak' matings (Bercovitch, 1997; Higham et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bercovitch, 1997 and Higham et al., 2011.

claim: In provisioned rhesus macaque populations, females typically have their first offspring between the ages of 3 and 5, and produce one offspring per year until reproduction slows as a result of senescence, typically around age 17.
source: In provisioned populations (both captive and free-ranging), females typically have their first offspring between the ages of 3 and 5, and produce one offspring per year until reproduction slows as a result of senescence, typically around age 17 (Lee et al., 2021; Pittet et al., 2017; Wilson et al., 1983).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: In wild, negligibly-provisioned Chinese rhesus macaques, the average age of first birth is 4.9 years old.
source: One study of wild negligibly-provisioned Chinese rhesus macaques found the average age of first birth to be 4.9 years old, approximately a year later than the average seen in food-supplemented populations (Tian et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Tian et al., 2013.

claim: Gestation length in rhesus macaques is approximately 166 days.
source: Gestation length in rhesus macaques is approximately 166 days, and sex ratio at birth is not significantly different from 1:1 (Fooden, 2000; Tian et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fooden, 2000 and Tian et al., 2015.

claim: Sex ratio at birth in rhesus macaques is not significantly different from 1:1.
source: Gestation length in rhesus macaques is approximately 166 days, and sex ratio at birth is not significantly different from 1:1 (Fooden, 2000; Tian et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fooden, 2000 and Tian et al., 2015.

claim: In wild-feeding rhesus macaque populations, annual birth rate per female is between 0.43 and 0.91.
source: Annual birth rate (births/sexually mature female) varies largely by population, and in wild-feeding populations annual birth rate per female is between 0.43 and 0.91 (Fooden, 2000)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fooden, 2000.

claim: Lower birth rates in rhesus macaques are associated with populations at the Northernmost edge of the natural range.
source: with lower birth rates associated with populations at the Northernmost edge of the natural range (e.g. Wenyuan et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wenyuan et al., 1993.

claim: On Cayo Santiago, female rhesus macaque reproductive output dropped significantly in years when the island was hit by a hurricane.
source: For example, on the island population of Cayo Santiago, female reproductive output dropped significantly in years when the island was hit by a hurricane (Morcillo et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Morcillo et al., 2020.

claim: Matrilineal overthrows in rhesus macaque societies result in significant infant loss for both the deposed and the attacking matrilines.
source: Additionally, matrilineal overthrows, a rare event in rhesus macaque societies where the highest-ranking matriline is violently overthrown by a lower ranking matriline, has been shown to result in significant infant loss for both the deposed and the attacking matrilines (Ehardt and Bernstein, 1986; Dettmer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ehardt and Bernstein, 1986 and Dettmer et al., 2015.

claim: For one rhesus macaque population at the northernmost limit of the species range, the main source of mortality was starvation or winter exposure to cold temperatures.
source: For one population at the northernmost limit of the species range, the main source of mortality was starvation or winter exposure to cold temperatures (Wenyuan et al., 1993)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wenyuan et al., 1993.

claim: Recorded predators of rhesus macaques include snakes, hawks and eagles, dogs, and large cats such as tigers and leopards.
source: Recorded predators of rhesus macaques include snakes (Seth and Seth, 1983), hawks and eagles (Lindburg, 1971; Wenyuan et al., 1993), dogs (Lindburg, 1971), and large cats such as tigers and leopards (Lovari et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Mortality due to wound complications such as tetanus infection following physical altercations may be a common cause of death in rhesus macaques.
source: Physical fighting between rhesus macaques can also be deadly, and mortality due to wound complications such as tetanus infection following physical altercations may be a common cause of death (Rawlins and Kessler, 1982).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rawlins and Kessler, 1982.

claim: Annual mortality has been reported between 2% and 10% for adult rhesus macaques, and between 7% and 32% for infants across different wild populations.
source: Annual mortality has been reported between 2% and 10% for adult rhesus macaques, and between 7% and 32% for infants across different wild populations (Fooden, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fooden, 2000.

claim: Male rhesus macaques have the highest mortality rate during the mating season, and females have the highest mortality rate during the birth season.
source: Males have the highest mortality rate during the mating season, and females have the highest mortality rate during the birth season, reflecting the sex-specific costs of reproduction (Hoffman et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hoffman et al., 2008.

claim: In captive populations under controlled conditions, rhesus macaques typically live for 25–30 years, and maximum lifespan has been recorded as 40 years.
source: In captive populations under controlled conditions, rhesus macaques typically live for 25–30 years, and maximum lifespan has been recorded as 40 years (Colman et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Colman et al., 2009.

claim: On Cayo Santiago, most adult female rhesus macaques die between 15 and 25 years of age, with the maximum recorded lifespan being 31.
source: Under the less controlled conditions of the free-ranging population on Cayo Santiago where rhesus macaques are provisioned and predator-free, but not given medical care, most adult females die between 15 and 25 years of age, with the maximum recorded lifespan being 31 (Hoffman et al., 2010; Maestripieri and Hoffman, 2011; Chiou et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Lifespan in wild rhesus macaques is likely to be considerably shorter than in provisioned populations and may be comparable to the averages of other cercopithecine monkeys of 10–15 years under natural conditions.
source: Lifespan in the wild is likely to be considerably shorter than under these conditions and may be comparable to the averages of other cercopithecine monkeys of 10–15 years under natural conditions (Maestripieri and Hoffman, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Maestripieri and Hoffman, 2012.

claim: Rhesus macaques have been described as 'weed macaques'.
source: Their persistence across a broad environmental range has long been recognized as a defining feature of the species, as evidenced by their description as 'weed macaques' (Maestripieri, 2008; Richard et al., 1989).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Maestripieri, 2008 and Richard et al., 1989.

claim: Rhesus macaques are increasingly being considered a 'pest' species.
source: While urbanization often results in the pushing out of endemic wildlife (McKinney, 2008; Savard et al., 2000), the opposite is true of rhesus macaques, as the species has been known to prefer habitats in urban and agricultural areas, leading to them increasingly being considered a 'pest' species (Saraswat et al., 2015; Sharma and Acharya, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Saraswat et al., 2015 and Sharma and Acharya, 2017.

claim: The rhesus macaque range stretches from Afghanistan in the west, through Pakistan, India, Nepal, Bangladesh, Bhutan, Myanmar, Thailand, Laos, Vietnam, and across a large swathe of China in the east.
source: Rhesus macaques (blue shaded area) have the largest natural range of any non-human primate, which stretches from Afghanistan in the west, through Pakistan, India, Nepal, Bangladesh, Bhutan, Myanmar, Thailand, Laos, Vietnam, and across a large swathe of China in the east.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2 caption and the map.
